Ramsey County offices for St. Paul owners

Ramsey County sends the St. Paul property tax bill. Its Assessor values every parcel, and its Property Tax Services unit mails the statements and takes the money. The county offices share the Plato Building at 90 Plato Blvd. West, Saint Paul, MN 55107, with front-desk service on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m. Direct lines worth saving:

  • Property Tax Services, 651-266-2222: statements, payments, penalties
  • County Assessor, 651-266-2131: value and classification
  • Homestead Unit, 651-266-2040: applications and ITIN filing
  • Delinquent taxes, 651-266-2002: balances, interest, plans
  • Recorder's Office, 651-266-2050: deeds and other recorded real estate documents

Keep the parcel number from your statement in front of you when you call. Each of these offices looks up records by that number.

Housing and classification in St. Paul

Owners and renters split the city almost evenly. Owners live in 52.9% of occupied homes, a typical owned home is valued at $294,500, and middle-market rent runs $1,281 a month. Owners with a mortgage spend $1,911 monthly.

Your bill hinges on classification. Ramsey County posts separate calculators for homestead and non-homestead houses, duplexes and triplexes, commercial buildings, and apartments of four or more units. Work out which category your parcel falls into before you estimate a tax figure for a buyer.

Due dates

Two installments, May 15 and October 15, cover real property, and a due date that falls on a weekend slides to Monday. Anyone with an escrow account at a mortgage company can skip the paperwork, since the lender pays. A bill of $100 or less must be settled whole with the first installment. October 15 has already passed this year, so a seller listing now should confirm the second half was paid.

When each kind of Ramsey County bill is due
TypeFirst installmentSecond installment
Real propertyMay 15October 15
AgriculturalMay 15October 15
Leased government-owned personal propertyMay 15October 15
Other personal propertyMay 15, total dueNone
Manufactured homesAugust 31November 15

Each property gets two mailings a year. Mid-March brings the tax statement together with the value notice that drives next year's tax. In November the proposed tax notice follows, listing next year's proposed amounts and the meetings where levies and budgets are discussed. Owners may switch to electronic delivery through eNoticesOnline.

What a late payment costs

Penalty starts the day after a due date, grows month by month, and is applied to penalty before tax when you pay. For a homestead or cabin, a late first half picks up 2% on May 16, 4% on June 1, 5% on July 1 and 8% by October 1, then 10% on January 2 of the next year. Non-homestead property climbs through 4%, 8%, 9% and 12% to 14% on those same dates.

A missed second half begins on October 16 at 2% for a homestead and 4% for a non-homestead, ending January 2 at 7% and 11%. Owing both halves on October 16 means 5% for a homestead and 8% otherwise.

The county offers two ways to soften a penalty:

  • One-time waiver: once per parcel in any 10-year span, for the first half or the second but not both. A first-half request must arrive from May 16 through October 15, and a second-half request from October 16 through December 20, with payment and the signed form. A waiver is refused if the payment bounced, if delinquent tax or a confession of judgment sits on the parcel, or if the waiver was already used in the past decade.
  • Hardship abatement: ask the County Auditor/Treasurer at 651-266-2222. The county grants these mainly for exceptional hardship such as a hospital stay.

Returned checks cost $30, and partial payments are accepted.

What can I do if I think my St. Paul value is wrong?

Phone the Assessor at 651-266-2131 before anything else. You will not reach an appraiser on the spot: you describe the concern, and an appraiser calls back within three days. Mail or email a recent appraisal or a sale of your own property to back a claim of overvaluation or a wrong class.

State law requires a physical review of each parcel at least once every five years, and Ramsey County appraisers walk nearly 32,000 properties a year without advance notice. An interactive map on the county site shows when your area is due.

Homestead status

Homestead status lowers the bill, so a seller and a buyer should both know the rules:

  • The state exclusion trims taxable value only on homes valued below $517,200.
  • Homestead also counts toward the state Property Tax Refund.
  • A buyer must own and occupy the home by December 31 and apply by that date to qualify for the current assessment year.
  • An ITIN may replace a Social Security number on the filing.

Delinquent tax and forfeiture

A bill becomes delinquent on January 1 of the next year. From then, interest accrues at 10% a year, rising monthly, and a $25 fee covers publication and notice. Owners then have three years to pay in full and redeem, or they can enter a payment plan called a Confession of Judgment.

If redemption lapses without payment, forfeiture begins, and the county notifies the owner in stages:

  • A courtesy letter in the first week of April
  • A parcel list in the county's newspaper for two weeks in May
  • The same list posted at the Property Records and Property Tax Services offices
  • Delivery of the notice by the sheriff to an occupant, or a posting at vacant and land-only property
  • A certified letter in June

Payments are applied to penalties first, then interest, fees and finally tax. A parcel may be paid after the list is printed, so call the delinquent line before assuming it is still on it.

Sell as-isNo repairs, no cleaning and no showings. We buy houses in any condition.See My Cash Offer →

Selling with taxes owed or open

Ask Property Tax Services for the parcel's exact balance, because the first half may be settled while the second is open, or both may be owed. Also ask where the account sits on the penalty schedule, since the rate steps up on June 1, July 1, October 16 and other dates. A cash buyer or a title company will want the same figure, so request it early in the listing period.

Deeds and similar papers are recorded through the Recorder's Office, which keeps the county's official real estate records. It does not help fill out legal forms. A recorded document is permanent and cannot be removed or altered, so have a title company or attorney review the deed before it is filed.

If the home sells for cash, the closing can move fast. The tax payoff, any penalty and any special items still have to be cleared at the table, which is why the balance request comes first.

Frequently asked questions

Which agency collects St. Paul's property tax?

Ramsey County Property Tax Services, in the Plato Building at 90 Plato Blvd. West. Reach it at 651-266-2222 on weekdays between 8 a.m. and 4:30 p.m.

When do St. Paul real property installments fall due?

May 15 and October 15. A weekend date moves to the next business day, and manufactured homes use August 31 and November 15 instead.

Is there a way to avoid a late St. Paul property tax penalty?

A one-time waiver exists, usable once per parcel every 10 years for one installment. Submit the signed form with your payment before the deadline for that half.

Who reviews a disputed St. Paul property value?

The County Assessor, at 651-266-2131. An appraiser returns your call within three days, and a recent appraisal or sale of the home can be sent as support.

What redemption window applies to delinquent tax on a St. Paul home?

Three years to pay everything owed, with payment plans available. The delinquent line, 651-266-2002, can give the current balance and interest.

Who sends the tax bill

A Rochester house is billed by Olmsted County. The county assessor decides what the property is worth for tax purposes, and one statement covers the levies of the county, the city, the schools and any special districts on your parcel.

Payments go to Olmsted County Property Records and Licensing at the Government Center, 151 4th Street SE, Rochester, MN 55904. Call 507-328-7636 about statements, 507-328-7635 about delinquent years, and 507-328-7670 for the assessor.

About 76,000 parcels countywide are valued as of each January 2, and state law ties the estimate to market value. Your value notice arrives in mid-March with the tax statement. The county's property assessments page covers the valuation side.

Rochester housing at a glance

Rochester has 124,292 residents, the third largest city in Minnesota, and its housing market follows the medical economy around Mayo Clinic. The typical owner-occupied home was worth $310,500 for 2020 to 2024, and 65.1% of households own their homes. Median gross rent is $1,399, and median owner cost with a mortgage is $1,864 a month. Older stock near downtown and newer subdivisions on the edges price very differently, so a recent comparable sale matters more than a citywide median.

Due dates and late penalties

Owners pay in two installments, one in mid-May and one in mid-October. Farmland second halves and manufactured home second halves fall on November 15, and the manufactured home first half is due August 31.

If an installment is still open on your parcel, the penalty schedule in Minnesota Statutes 279.01 applies. Late fees start at 2 percent for a homestead and 4 percent for everything else, double once the next month begins, and then add 1 percent per month until they reach 8 percent (homestead) or 12 percent (other property).

Two details help when a payment is close to the line. Bills of $100 or under come due in one lump on May 15. And the statute gives a one-time break: a mailed check postmarked no more than one business day late can have its penalty erased, once per owner. If you mail near a deadline, ask a postal clerk for a hand-applied postmark.

December 15Homestead applications due
Free, no-obligation offerTell us about your house and get a written cash offer within 24 hours.Get My Cash Offer →

Ways to pay

Whichever method you choose, quote the parcel ID from your statement. A real property ID looks like RP 74.05.05.000000.

  • Online, on the county's property information site: card at 3.28 percent or e-check at $3.16, current year only, capped at $300,000. Allow seven to 10 business days for the bank to clear it and wait for the confirmation email.
  • Phone: 1-800-272-9829, jurisdiction number 3336. This line also takes back-year tax at the same rates.
  • Mail: check or money order made out to Olmsted County, with the stub, and five to seven business days of postal transit.
  • Counter: cash, check, money order or card at the Government Center, where cards add 2.15 percent. Drop boxes are there too.
  • Your bank's bill pay: the parcel ID serves as the account number, and the county counts the day it receives the money.

A free ACH withdrawal program is also available. Sign-up cutoffs come in April for the May draft and in September for the October draft, with money pulled on the 10th of May and October. Selling can end an enrollment, judged by the date the deed is recorded, so tell the office in writing if a sale lands near a withdrawal.

How to challenge your valuation

Begin with the assessor's office at 507-328-7670, carrying a recent appraisal or sale prices of comparable homes.

Still unsettled? Attend a meeting from the schedule on your valuation notice. Places with their own local board start there, and the rest go directly to the county board. By statute, local boards sit between April 1 and May 31 and can lower the assessor's overall total by no more than 1 percent. The county board follows in mid-June.

The last step is the Minnesota Tax Court, with a petition due by April 30 of the year the tax is payable. A 2023 change also requires a copy to reach the county auditor. Olmsted County takes that copy by email at olmcotaxpetitionservice@olmstedcounty.gov or by hand at the County Attorney's Office. The Tax Court's phone number is 651-539-3260.

Relief programs that can lower your tax

State programs do most of the work. Homestead applications are due December 15 and exempt property applications February 1. Green Acres applications for farmland are due May 1.

  • Regular property tax refund, often called the circuit breaker, based on household income and the tax you pay.
  • Special refund, available when net tax rises by at least 12 percent and $100, with no income test. Both refunds use Form M1PR.
  • Senior citizen property tax deferral, applied for through the Minnesota Department of Revenue on Form CR-SCD.
  • Credit of $120 per month served for members of the military in a combat zone or hazardous duty area.

Notices of proposed taxes, the Truth in Taxation mailing, go out in mid-November. They project next year's bill if each taxing body adopts the budget now on the table, and they list hearing dates.

Selling with taxes owed

A past-due balance stays with the parcel, so ask the county for the exact payoff at 507-328-7635 before closing. Taxes left unpaid long enough can lead to forfeiture, with title passing to the State of Minnesota.

A sale also changes who gets the mail. The county sends one statement a year in late March, to the address you gave at closing, and sends none for mid-year purchases. Tax information may also show up in your closing papers. Once a deed is recorded, the assessor removes homestead status from the next assessment year unless the new owner applies and qualifies (Minnesota Statutes 272.115).

If your Rochester house has tax behind and you want a quick sale, pull together the parcel ID, your latest statement and the payoff figure first. If automatic withdrawal is on, send the county a written stop request, since a recorded transfer may end it only after the recording date. A buyer paying cash can close fast, but the payoff still has to be settled at the table.

Frequently asked questions

Who collects property tax in Rochester, MN?

Olmsted County Property Records and Licensing takes the payments, and the county assessor sets values. For statement questions call 507-328-7636.

What happens if I miss the second-half Rochester property tax payment?

Penalties start at 2 percent for a homestead and 4 percent for other property, and they grow each month. Farm and manufactured home second halves are due November 15.

Can I pay Rochester property tax by credit card?

Yes. Card payments online or by phone add 3.28 percent, and an e-check adds $3.16. At the Government Center counter the card surcharge is 2.15 percent.

How do I get a copy of my Rochester tax statement?

Print one from the county's property information website or call 507-328-7636. Reprints at the office cost $2.

Does automatic withdrawal stop when I sell my Rochester home?

Not always right away. A transfer of the property may end the enrollment, but timing follows the recording date of the deed. Tell the county in writing if a withdrawal date is near.
